title: Late-binding subtokenizer + hierarchical session cache to reduce prefill overhead
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem statement:
Current prefill pipeline pays substantial per-request CPU overhead for full-token segmentation and UTF8-normalization even when much of the prompt overlaps previous session prefixes. This increases p50/p95 prefill latency and wastes host CPU cycles under high QPS, which cascades into higher kernel scheduling contention and reduced GPU utilization.

Goal:
Introduce a late-binding, subtoken-aware segmentation stage combined with a small hierarchical session cache that: (1) avoids full re-tokenization of common prefixes, (2) supports byte-granular substring match for mid-prompt edits, and (3) provides a lightweight fast-path for short CTAs and structured prompts. Target: reduce median prefill CPU wall time by 35% and p95 latency by 20% for typical PLG traffic (short prompts + session prefixes).

Design overview:
- Late-binding subtokenizer: postpone expensive normalization and subtoken merging until we know batch membership and routing decisions. Produce a compact intermediate form (byte-range hashes + small metadata) per request so that we can cheaply compare and stitch cached pieces without a full re-run of the tokenizer logic.
- Hierarchical session cache: multi-tier cache keyed by (customer_id, model_family, session_prefix_hash) with two tiers: L1 in-process small ring buffer for hot sessions (per-worker), and L2 shared in-memory shard (per-host) for less-hot items. Both store intermediate subtoken slices with token count metadata and KV-cache hints.
- Fast-path heuristics: detect three classes of requests at ingest: Prefix-only (exact match), Prefix+small delta (byte-edit distance below threshold), and New (no cache). Route Prefix-only immediately to a cheap stitch path that increments token counters and returns compiled KV-fill instructions; Prefix+small delta will run a micro-segmentation only on the changed byte ranges.
- Interaction with kernel selection & scheduling: the runtime will expose an indicator (prefill_fastpath) to the scheduler so that requests that fully hit the stitch path can be batched into low-latency queues with different kernel selection heuristics (favor single-GPU microbatches and attention-kernel tuned for short sequences).

Trade-offs considered:
- Cache memory vs CPU: L1 cache keeps very small entries (<1KB) to avoid memory blowup; L2 entries are size-limited and evicted on LRU. This reduces some cache hit-rate vs storing full token lists but keeps host memory stable.
- Correctness vs performance: the stitch path is conservative and falls back to full tokenization when any ambiguous Unicode normalization or tokenizer-edge cases occur. We prefer a 'slow and correct' fallback over occasional mismatches.
- Complexity: adds bookkeeping in session lifecycle and eviction; initial rollout will gate behind a runtime flag and model whitelist to limit blast radius.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Prototype intermediate representation and micro-stitching algorithm in Go (tokenizer-service branch).
2) Implement L1 ring buffer (lock-free per-worker) + L2 host shard (sharded map) with metrics.
3) Add heuristic classifier at ingest; add runtime flag and model whitelist config.
4) Integrate with scheduler API: emit prefill_fastpath hints and request class to scheduler for kernel selection.
5) End-to-end benchmark and correctness fuzz tests (see test plan).
6) Gradual rollout: 1% traffic -> 10% -> 50% -> global, with canary telemetry.

Benchmarks & success metrics (initial local runs):
- Microbench harness (short prompts, 8k QPS emulation): median prefill CPU time from 3.2ms -> 1.9ms (≈41% improvement); p95 from 9.8ms -> 7.6ms (≈22% improvement).
- End-to-end p50 latency for short chat flows on a dedicated node: 18ms -> 13ms.
- GPU utilization improvement measured as fewer kernel preempts when prefill CPU drops under threshold.

Test plan & validation:
- Unit tests for stitcher correctness across Unicode edge cases and multi-byte edits.
- Fuzz harness that mutates session prefixes and validates decode outputs against baseline full-tokenizer path.
- Load test in staging with realistic PLG traffic trace (trace anonymized, stored in S3: s3://redwood-traces/prefill/2026-02-sample.json).
- Canary with runtime flag and telemetry capturing cache hit-rate, stitch-to-fallback ratio, end-to-end latency, and decode quality diffs (BLEU/ROUGE-like token-level checks and sample human review for 100 cases).

Docs & rollout artifacts:
- PRD: internal doc at https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Late-Binding+Subtokenizer (draft)
- Design notes and algorithm pseudocode: gdoc https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xyz-prefill-stitcher
- Prototype PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1289

Open questions / risks to address in next iteration:
- Optimal hash granularity (byte-range length) — current prototype uses 16B rolling windows; may tune to reduce collisions.
- Eviction policies for cross-tenant fairness under noisy neighbors. Consider token-count-weighted eviction or customer QoS reservations.
- Scheduler coupling: need to ensure runtime hints don't starve default scheduling classes. We'll add safety limits on fastpath batch sizes.

Next steps (short-term):
- Finish prototype PR and run staging load tests (owner: Rafael).
- Add integration tests that validate kernel selection annotation is respected by scheduler (owner: infra-scheduler).
- Prepare rollout playbook and monitoring dashboards (owner: observability).
